## Eight practitioner assumptions, negated

| # | Assumption | Negation → implied conditional |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | A skip on the 0→3 shortcut makes deeper convs on other paths safer. | Negated: the shortcut makes them redundant. Conv upgrades on edges 4 and 5 would gain **less** when edge 3 is skip, and more when it is none. |
| A2 | Stacking convs in series compounds receptive field, so a conv edit gains more after an upstream conv. | Negated: it saturates. Conv3x3 on edge 2 would gain less after a conv3x3 on edge 0. Pool-after-pool should hurt more than the pool edit's average. |
| A3 | Parallel convs into one node add complementary capacity. | Negated: they are redundant. A conv edit on edge 1 or 2 would gain less when its sibling is already conv3x3. |
| A4 | Avg-pool is a weak, redundant op. | Negated: it complements a parallel conv. Adding pool on edge 1 would gain more when edge 2 is conv3x3. |
| A5 | Replacing `none` and replacing `avg_pool` with the same op give similar gains. | Negated: replacing `none` adds a path, while replacing pool only swaps one. Skip or conv gains would be larger where `none` is replaced (k = j). |
| A6 | Sparse cells are fragile, so each surviving edge matters less than the connectivity itself. | Negated: survivors carry more load. Upgrading an edge to conv would gain more when a sibling edge is `none`. |
| A7 | Cutting the first edge (edge 0 = none) simply removes one path. | Negated: it disables the whole 0→1 chain. Downstream edits on edges 4 and 5 would gain **less**, because their input is gone. |
| A8 | Skip edges are always benign. | Negated: skip is redundant next to existing deep or conv paths. Adding skip on edge 3 would gain less when edges 4 or 5 are already conv, and more when they are none. |
